text: 1. Introduction
label: heading

text: Mobile devices, smartphones and tablet computers in particular, have generated a lot of
label: paragraph

text: interest among researchers in recent years (Byrne & Diem, 2014). This is because the
label: paragraph

text: opportunities these new technologies may offer (e.g. individualized learning, the variety
label: paragraph

text: of mobile apps available, easy access to the internet) and/or the fact that they are
label: paragraph

text: increasingly more common among learners make them an important and potentially
label: paragraph

text: useful addition to formal and informal language learning.
label: paragraph

text: According to Benson (2011), there has always been a connection between educational
label: paragraph

text: technologies and learner autonomy to the extent that they have often been intended for
label: paragraph

text: independent practice. It should be noted, however, that this link and “future enquiry
label: paragraph

text: and practice into technology-mediated learner autonomy will need to be increasingly
label: paragraph

text: aligned to the tools, settings, and activities that are of significance to language learne
label: paragraph

text: (Reinders & White, 2016, p. 151). Reinders and White (2016) further argue that as long
label: paragraph

text: as “the potential range of settings, tools, and experiences is now virtually limitless,
label: paragraph

text: individuals need to be increasingly adept at critical adaptive learning in order to benefi
label: paragraph

text: from and contribute effectively to those settings” (p. 151). Beyond doubt, contemporary
label: paragraph

text: language teachers should equip foreign/second language learners with appropriate
label: paragraph

text: knowledge concerning the affordances of mobile devices for language study and they
label: paragraph

label: paragraph

label: paragraph

text: 2. Literature review
label: heading

text: 2.1. Autonomy in foreign/second language learning
label: paragraph

text: The concept of autonomy in second/foreign language learning and teaching has been
label: paragraph

text: the focus of attention for many researchers and practitioners for more than three
label: paragraph

text: decades. According to Benson (2001), the notion of autonomy was introduced and
label: paragraph

text: popularized in 1981 by Henri Holec in his seminal report for the Council of Europe
label: paragraph

text: entitled Autonomy in Foreign Language Learning in which the researcher defined
label: paragraph

text: autonomy in the context of language learning as “the ability to take charge of one’s own
label: paragraph

text: learning” (Holec, 1981, p. 3). Holec’s idea of autonomy encompasses some components
label: paragraph

text: and capacities on the part of language learners (e.g. self-directed learning). For some
label: paragraph

text: other authors autonomy also involves “a capacity – for detachment, critical reflection,
label: paragraph

text: decision-making, and independent action” (Little, 1991, p. 4) and “the capacity to take
label: paragraph

text: control of one’s own learning” (Benson, 2001, p. 46). As stated by Benson (2011, p.
label: paragraph

text: 16), “autonomy is multidimensional and takes many different forms according to the
label: paragraph

text: person, the setting, and multiple contextual and micro-contextual factors” and it is “a
label: paragraph

text: multi-faceted concept that consists of several layers” (Reinders, 2011, p. 48) whose
label: paragraph

text: roots are based in political, societal and educational developments. In addition to this,
label: paragraph

text: work on autonomy emphasizes social dimensions of learner autonomy in view of the
label: paragraph

text: fact that “autonomous learners always do things for themselves, but they may or may
label: paragraph

text: not do things on their own” (Little, 2009, p. 223) and that by means of social
label: paragraph

text: interactions language learners “develop a capacity to analyze, reflect upon and
label: paragraph

text: synthesize information to create new perspectives” (Lee, 2011, p. 88). It should also be
label: paragraph

text: noted that recent research shows that fostering autonomy is no longer predominantly a
label: paragraph

text: matter of individualizing learning through out-of-class initiatives since the dominance of
label: paragraph

text: classroom-based approaches (Benson, 2011). Finally, it has to be added that
label: paragraph

text: researchers, in general, seem to be in agreement with the following claims suggested
label: paragraph

text: by Benson (2011): “(a) language learners naturally tend to take control of their
label: paragraph

text: learning, (b) learners who lack autonomy are capable of developing it, and (c)
label: paragraph

text: autonomous language learning is more effective than non-autonomous language
label: paragraph

text: learning” (p. 16).
label: paragraph

text: Perhaps in order to define the concept of autonomy in language learning it is necessary
label: paragraph

text: to understand who autonomous learners are. As Littlewood (1996) claims, an
label: paragraph

text: autonomous learner is “one who has independent capacity to make and carry out
label: paragraph

text: choices which govern his or her actions” (p. 428). The researcher argues that this
label: paragraph

text: capacity depends on two major components such as ability and willingness, and he
label: paragraph

text: claims that the attributes can also be further subdivided. Thus, ability depends on
label: paragraph

text: having knowledge about the options from which one can choose and skills so as to
label: paragraph

text: choose the most suitable alternatives. When it comes to willingness, this depends on
label: paragraph

text: having motivation and confidence in order to take responsibility for adequate choices.
label: paragraph

text: Moreover, Littlewood (1996) argues that if an individual is to be successful in being
label: paragraph

text: autonomous, all of these components have to be present all together.
label: paragraph

text: At the close of this section, a few words are in order on the notion of autonomous
label: paragraph

text: language learning. An interesting description of the concept in question is offered by
label: paragraph

text: Reinders (2011), who defines autonomous language learning as “an act of learning
label: paragraph

text: whereby motivated learners consciously make informed decisions about that learning”
label: paragraph

text: (p. 48). According to the said researcher, it is not possible or needed in all acts of
label: paragraph

text: learning to be able or ready to intentionally make decisions since different learning
label: paragraph

text: situations present different demands. Reinders (2011) further argues that “autonomy is
label: paragraph

text: not an either-or concept, but has to be seen as a continuum” (p. 48). This is because a
label: paragraph

text: learner can display more or less autonomy in different learning circumstances.
label: paragraph

text: Autonomy, in Reinders’ terms changes over time between skills and within skills and
label: paragraph

text: thus it is difficult to achieve and is not invariably permanent (Reinders, 2011).

text: 2.2. Autonomy and new technologies
label: paragraph

text: As stated in the previous section, the concept of autonomy has been one of the most
label: paragraph

text: researched areas in the field of second/foreign language learning and teaching over the
label: paragraph

text: last few decades. It should be noted, however, that the field of learner autonomy
label: paragraph

text: started to be influenced by technology in the mid-1990s as a result of the growing
label: paragraph

text: influence of the internet on almost every sphere of our life (including second/foreign
label: paragraph

text: language education) and the opportunities for online collaboration and communication
label: paragraph

text: (Reinders & White, 2016). As stated by Benson and Chik (2010), the latest generations
label: paragraph

text: of new technologies, particularly those encompassing the internet, user-generated Web
label: paragraph

text: content and mobility, seem to be having a bearing on the way autonomous language
label: paragraph

text: learning develops. Perhaps, one of the most important benefits of implementing new
label: paragraph

text: technologies into language learning is the fact that they provide occasions for language
label: paragraph

text: learners who do not have direct access to the target language. This is because the use
label: paragraph

text: of new technologies, including mobile technology, allow them to “bypass classrooms and
label: paragraph

text: go directly to target language texts and users through the internet and social media”
label: paragraph

text: When it comes to the use of mobile technology, and, in particular, smartphones and
label: paragraph

text: tablet computers, for learning a foreign or second language, they can assist language
label: paragraph

text: learners with their learning endeavors by granting access to numerous language
label: paragraph

text: resources whenever and wherever such learners need them and/or they happen to be
label: paragraph

text: (Jones, 2015). In Jones’s opinion, such language involvement might comprise, for
label: paragraph

text: instance, the use of chunks of spare time for language practice, searching for target
label: paragraph

text: language vocabulary in relevant contexts or interactions on social media (Jones, 2015).
label: paragraph

text: Furthermore, by having a mobile device a language learner has the opportunity to take
label: paragraph

text: control of his or her learning, direct it and engage in language activities that meet his
label: paragraph

text: her individual needs and goals (Kukulska-Hulme, Traxler & Pettit, 2007; Pettit &
label: paragraph

text: Kukulska-Hulme 2007).

text: 3.1. Research question
label: paragraph

text: One of the questions related to future research and practice in technology-mediated
label: paragraph

text: learner autonomy addressed by Reinders and White in their recent critical overview of
label: paragraph

text: the relationship between technology and autonomy in the journal Language Learning &
label: paragraph

text: Technology (LLT) concerned language learners engagement with technology-mediated
label: paragraph

text: environments in order to develop learning experiences that reach their aims and meet
label: paragraph

text: their needs as language learners (Reinders & White, 2016). Taking this important
label: paragraph

text: matter into consideration, and in view of the fact that mobile technology, including
label: paragraph

text: mobile devices such as smartphones and tablet computers, are ubiquitous and
label: paragraph

text: substantial constituents of almost every language learner’s everyday life, the
label: paragraph

text: abovementioned question was modified and posed in this study in the following way:
label: paragraph

text: Do students engage with their mobile devices to develop learning experiences
label: paragraph

label: paragraph

text: study) that meet their needs and goals (e.g. the development of the target
label: paragraph

text: language skills and sub-skills) as English language learners? If yes, why and how
label: paragraph

text: do they do this?

text: 3.3. Data collection and analysis
label: paragraph

text: The data were gathered by means of a semi-structured interview. This interview format
label: paragraph

text: was chosen intentionally since it uses a set of prepared in advance guiding questions
label: paragraph

text: and prompts and interviewees are encouraged to elaborate on the problems raised
label: paragraph

text: during it (Dörnyei, 2007). As Dörnyei (2007) explains, in this type of the interview “the
label: paragraph

text: interviewer provides guidelines and direction (hence the ‘-structured’ part in the name),
label: paragraph

text: but is also keen to follow up interesting developments and to let the interviewee
label: paragraph

text: elaborate on certain issues (hence the ‘semi-’ part)” (p. 136).
label: paragraph

label: paragraph

text: describe their learning experiences concerning the use of mobile devices for English
label: paragraph

label: paragraph

label: paragraph

label: paragraph

text: 5. Discussion and conclusions
label: heading

text: The picture that emerges from the analysis of the collected data regarding the advanced
label: paragraph

text: learners' use of mobile devices for learning English is relatively encouraging. This is
label: paragraph

text: because all the study participants used, at least to some extent, their mobile devices
label: paragraph

text: (i.e. smartphones and/or tablet computers) in order to learn the English language
label: paragraph

text: autonomously. Moreover, the positive impact of using mobile devices for English study
label: paragraph

text: was acknowledged by the majority of the interviewees. Their beneficial contribution to
label: paragraph

text: their English development was chiefly linked with easy access to English language
label: paragraph

text: resources, the opportunity to store them, comfort in using their smartphones and
label: paragraph

text: tablets anywhere and anytime as well as perceived gains in English learning. The results
label: paragraph

text: of the study also showed that all interviewees engaged with their smartphones and/or
label: paragraph

text: tablet computers to practice the target language vocabulary (plus some students also
label: paragraph

text: claimed to learn pronunciation of English words) and the majority of the subjects used
label: paragraph

text: their mobile devices autonomously in their leisure time as well as during language
label: paragraph

text: classes. Such a state of affairs can be explained in terms of increased awareness on the
label: paragraph

text: part of some students of the beneficial role of MobDs in foreign language learning, their
label: paragraph

text: ability to reach for appropriate tools and retrieve needed information to achieve their
label: paragraph

text: goals and adjust their learning of the target language to their personal learning styles.
label: paragraph

text: Despite this positive view of MobDs reported by the study participants, the results of the
label: paragraph

text: study also revealed that only a few subjects engaged with their mobile devices to
label: paragraph

text: master target language skills such as reading, listening, writing and speaking as well as
label: paragraph

text: English language grammar. In addition, some interviewees limited themselves to a
label: paragraph

text: rather intuitive and perhaps even spontaneous use of their mobile devices in the
label: paragraph

text: language classroom. It should also be noted that almost half of the subjects regarded
label: paragraph

text: themselves as quite inexperienced in using their mobile devices when it comes to
label: paragraph

text: learning the English language despite the fact that some of the students had been using
label: paragraph

text: them with the intention of learning English for years. Taking all these findings into
label: paragraph

text: account, one may conclude that this is due to a failure or underestimation of the role
label: paragraph

text: and place of mobile devices in foreign language learning and teaching on the part of
label: paragraph

text: language teachers. It seems therefore warranted to say that the subjects’ use of mobile
label: paragraph

text: devices could be altered if teachers took into account the benefits they may offer. For
label: paragraph

text: this reason language teachers should, for instance, present the affordances of mobile
label: paragraph

text: technology and discuss them with students during language classes. They should also
label: paragraph

text: select mobile apps and create opportunities for using them in- and out-of-class learning
label: paragraph

text: by offering or designing tasks devoted to practicing a variety of language skills and
label: paragraph

text: subsystems suitable for the use of such devices. If this were to happen, teachers need
label: paragraph

text: to respond quickly to the constant and dynamic changes in contemporary
label: paragraph

text: foreign/second language learning and teaching contexts by undergoing official teacher
label: paragraph

text: training not only in the area of technology-mediated language learning and teaching but
label: paragraph

text: also in the context of learner autonomy.

label: paragraph

label: paragraph

text: related to the fact that the group was largely homogenous, i.e. the subjects came from
label: paragraph
